hints: Focus on the type of halogenoalkane first, since tertiary bromoalkanes strongly favour one nucleophilic substitution mechanism.
Recall that an SN1 pathway has two separate steps, so its energy profile shows a valley for the carbocation intermediate between two peaks for transition states.
Check which labelled point is a peak and which is a valley, then match the valley to the stable intermediate and the peaks to the bond-breaking or bond-making transition states.
walkthrough:
**Identify the mechanism from tertiary structure**

A tertiary bromoalkane is bulky and forms a stable tertiary carbocation. So it reacts with $\text{OH}^-$ by $\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$, not $\text{S}_{\text{N}}2$.

$$ \text{>C-Br} \rightarrow \text{>C}^+ + \text{Br}^- \text{ then } \text{>C}^+ + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{>C-OH} $$

**Recall what peaks and valleys mean**

On an energy profile, peaks are transition states (highest energy, bonds partly broken or formed). Valleys between peaks are intermediates (temporary but real species).

$$ \text{peak = transition state, valley = intermediate} $$

**Apply this to X and Y**

Here X is the first peak, so it is the transition state as the $\text{C-Br}$ bond breaks. Y is the valley after that, so it is the carbocation intermediate $\text{>C}^+ + \text{Br}^- + \text{OH}^-$ waiting to be attacked.

The second peak is then the transition state as the $\text{C-OH}$ bond forms.

**Rule out the SN2 structure**

The structure $\left[ \text{HO} \cdots \text{C} \cdots \text{Br} \right]^-$ is the single concerted transition state for $\text{S}_{\text{N}}2$. A tertiary halogenoalkane does not go through this, and an $\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$ profile never has both $\text{OH}$ and $\text{Br}$ attached in one transition state.

options.A: Incorrect. X is a peak, so it is a transition state, not an intermediate. The carbocation $\text{>C}^+$ sits in the energy valley, not on top of the energy hill.
options.B: Incorrect. $\left[ \text{HO} \cdots \text{C} \cdots \text{Br} \right]^-$ is the SN2 transition state where OH forms a bond at the same time Br leaves. Tertiary bromoalkanes react by SN1 in two separate steps, so this concerted structure does not occur.
options.C: Correct. Y is the valley (intermediate) after loss of $\text{Br}^-$. In SN1 this is the planar tertiary carbocation $\text{>C}^+$, which is then rapidly attacked by $\text{OH}^-$ in the second step.
options.D: Incorrect. Y is a valley, so it must be a stable intermediate, not a transition state. The $\left[ \text{HO} \cdots \text{C} \cdots \text{Br} \right]^-$ species belongs to SN2 and would appear as a peak, not a valley, and does not form here.
